Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse tasks (2D synthetic, image interpolation, video frame interpolation) with multiple metrics and datasets
Consistent improvements across FID, PPL, PDV, and RE metrics on all evaluated datasets

Theoretical contributions are straightforward: Proposition 1 is intuitive once stated; using J^T J for metrics is conventional; novelty lies mainly in application context

Unable to operate at t=0 (clean data space) due to metric degeneracy, limiting applicability in certain scenarios

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear presentation and intuitive illustrations showing limitations of existing interpolation methods
Theoretically grounded in recent findings about Jacobian structure encoding manifold information; provides multiple interpretations of the metric
Practical design requiring no architectural modifications or retraining, applicable to pre-trained diffusion models
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning synthetic data, multiple image datasets (MorphBench, Animal Faces-HQ, CelebA-HQ), and video frame interpolation with ground-truth evaluation
Consistent empirical improvements across metrics (FID, PPL, PDV, RE) with particularly good detail preservation in qualitative results
Ablation study on prompt adjustment demonstrates sensitivity and impact of design choices
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: using G = J^T J is a straightforward application of standard SVD properties. Proposition 1 (minimizing ||Jv||² favors tangent directions) is unsurprising linear algebra; proof assumes exact score function (symmetric Jacobian), but networks learn approximations, weakening claims

Critical missing analysis: no timing comparisons, computational complexity analysis, or runtime results despite acknowledging higher cost than LERP/SLERP. Geodesic optimization requires 500 iterations but convergence behavior is unanalyzed—this is a major practical concern for an interpolation method

Severely limited applicability: metric only works for t > 0 (breaks down at clean data); timestep τ empirically chosen with strong sensitivity (Fig. 7-8) and no principled selection method; only tested on single model (Stable Diffusion v2.1-base) with no generalization evidence

Weak metric design justification: no ablation studies comparing G = J^T J to alternatives; regularized version dismissed with vague 'preliminary experiments showed no effect'; use of modified score under CFG (Eq. 8) is ad-hoc without analyzing manifold-preservation

Geodesic computation issues unaddressed: non-convex optimization with no convergence analysis, guarantees, or sensitivity studies; initialization with SLERP could bias results; no stopping criteria or local minima detection discussed

Comparison methodology concerns: prompt adjustment adopted from GeoDiff but applied uniformly; NAO and NoiseDiff show surprisingly large errors suggesting implementation quality issues; GeoDiff (most competitive baseline) also requires optimization but computational costs aren't compared

Evaluation limitations: image interpolation lacks ground truth (proxy metrics can mislead); video uses only 3-frame setting; datasets limited to faces/animals (homogeneous); visual quality assessment subjective without user studies; results often modest vs GeoDiff (FID: 27.44 vs 28.70 on AF)

Missing critical ablations: no sensitivity analysis for discretization points N, iteration count, learning rate, optimizer choice, initialization strategies, or regularization strength. Reproducibility compromised by multiple unguided hyperparameters

Generalization concerns: limited to single model and homogeneous image domains; complex natural scenes, diverse datasets, and different architectures untested; metric quality depends on spectral gap but no systematic analysis provided

Overclaimed results: captions claim method 'runs parallel to manifold' without formal justification; claims about preserving 'underlying semantics' lack quantitative support; 'approximately holds' caveat for non-exact case undermines Proposition 1

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical contribution connecting Jacobian degeneracy to data manifold structure, building on recent foundational work with clear Proposition 1
Comprehensive experimental validation across synthetic data, image interpolation (three datasets), and video frame interpolation with ground-truth comparisons
Consistent empirical improvements over strong baselines including GeoDiff across multiple metrics (FID, PPL, RE, LPIPS, MSE)
Practical applicability: works with pre-trained models without retraining or architectural modifications; handles classifier-free guidance naturally
Clear problem formulation and presentation with effective motivation (Figure 1), thorough appendices, and reproducible code provided
No additional training required; method directly leverages geometry learned by existing diffusion models

Computational cost inadequately addressed: requires 500 Adam optimization iterations per interpolation path with no runtime comparisons provided; claimed comparability to GeoDiff lacks quantitative evidence; much slower than closed-form LERP/SLERP

Incremental improvements over strongest baseline: modest gains on CelebA-HQ (FID 32.54 vs 35.98 for GeoDiff, ~9%), smaller on other datasets (~4% on MB(A)); lacks statistical significance testing or confidence intervals

Critical hyperparameter τ ∈ [0.4T, 0.6T] is empirically determined without theoretical guidance; Figure 8 provides post-hoc justification via spectral gap analysis but offers no principled selection method for new models/datasets

Limited experimental scope: only image and video interpolation tested despite abstract mentioning 'editing'; only Stable Diffusion v2.1-base evaluated; generalization to other architectures and training paradigms unknown

Method requires 'reasonably good initialization' (noted in limitations) using SLERP; sensitivity to initialization quality not systematically studied; failure modes at t=0 shown but not thoroughly analyzed

Claim about manifold alignment is somewhat indirect: paper criticizes density-based methods for not following the true manifold but provides only indirect evidence (better perceptual quality) that proposed metric actually follows the data manifold vs. produces improved images through other mechanisms

Missing ablations: sensitivity to discretization points N, optimization iterations, initialization schemes; prompt adjustment (Appendix B.3) adopted from prior work without clear separation of its contribution

Thorough experimental documentation with extensive appendices covering alternative constructions, computational costs, hyperparameter sensitivity, and additional datasets

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical foundation connecting the Jacobian spectral structure to data manifold geometry through a principled Riemannian metric
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (2D synthetic, image/video interpolation on 7+ datasets) with consistent improvements and statistical significance testing

Clear mathematical exposition of the metric definition and geodesic-based algorithms with detailed appendices
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: primarily applies existing Jacobian observations (Stanczuk et al. 2024; Ventura et al. 2025) as a Riemannian metric; Proposition 1 is straightforward

Marginal practical improvements despite high computational cost: Table 2 shows gains <0.05 over FIM-based baseline; Table 6 indicates cost substantially higher than alternatives (N·S + T/ε + I + O(1)) making cost-benefit trade-off unfavorable

Weak theory-practice connection for guidance: tangent-normal decomposition is theoretically sound but its necessity for practical guidance is unclear; visual differences in Figure 8 are subtle and don't obviously justify added complexity

Hyperparameter proliferation without principled selection: τ=0.67 chosen empirically; CG iterations, prompt weight ω, and regularization λ require tuning; adds complexity for practitioners without clear guidance

Experimental concerns: most experiments on Stable Diffusion v2.1-base limiting generalization claims; differences from GeoDiff often <0.02 (within noise margins); guidance improvements may reflect implementation details rather than fundamental advantages; limited ablations on necessity of tangent-normal decomposition

strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: The insight that the Jacobian of the score function encodes data manifold geometry is clever and well-founded, with rigorous mathematical derivation.
Strong mathematical foundation: Clear connections to differential geometry, proper proofs (Proposition 1), and elegant formulation of the Riemannian metric.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive experiments across multiple domains (synthetic data, 4 image interpolation datasets, 3 video benchmarks) with proper statistical significance testing (p < 0.01).
Training-free practical method: Applicable to pre-trained models without modification or additional training, enabling immediate real-world deployment.
Thorough ablation studies: Detailed analysis of hyperparameter sensitivity (spectral gap τ, regularization λ, CG iterations) demonstrating robustness and providing insights.
Excellent presentation: Clear writing, effective geometric visualizations (Figures 1-4), and good balance between mathematical rigor and intuition.
Consistent improvements: Statistically significant gains across multiple metrics and datasets (e.g., best FID and RE scores on image interpolation, best MSE and LPIPS on video).
weaknesses: Computational overhead under-addressed: DDIM inversion, multiple score function evaluations, and iterative optimization add significant cost; no wall-clock time comparisons or real-time deployment feasibility analysis provided.
Incremental improvements in primary application: Image interpolation gains are modest (~1-2% on PPL, marginal on FID/PDV/RE), though guidance correction shows stronger improvements.

Jacobian symmetry assumption insufficiently justified: Critical assumption in Section B.1 lacks empirical validation across datasets; no analysis of approximation error or failure modes when J_θ is not symmetric.

Limited application scope demonstrated: Only two applications (interpolation and guidance correction) shown; broader utility of discovered geometry unexplored; no investigation of other manifold operations.
Manifold existence assumption under-examined: No discussion of when low-dimensional manifold assumption breaks down; real-world data may not satisfy this uniformly.
Hyperparameter selection lacks guidance: Spectral gap τ requires task-specific tuning (0.67 for images vs 0.47 for video) with no principled selection method for new datasets.
Sparse discussion of failure modes: Missing analysis of when staying tangential might be suboptimal or when the method should not be applied.
Missing recent comparisons: Several recent manifold-aware and geometry-aware diffusion methods not compared; incomplete coverage of related geometric approaches.
